summary: Standard guidance steers a diffusion model towards a single condition; Jeffrey guidance instead moves a whole marginal p(y) of some feature y = u(x) to a prescribed target p*(y) while keeping p(x|y) fixed, which by Jeffrey's rule gives p*(x) = ρ(u(x)) p(x) with ρ = p*/p. The density ratio ρ is estimated with a classifier separating target from model samples, and its gradient (evaluated at the Tweedie estimate x̂₀) is added to the score late in sampling. Matching Inception-embedding distributions cuts FID substantially on CIFAR-10 and FFHQ, and on CelebA-HQ it rebalances or decorrelates attributes.
takeaways: Jeffrey's rule is the minimal update of a joint that imposes a new marginal (an information projection); ordinary conditioning is the special case where p*(y) is a point mass.

With a deterministic feature map the target is an exponential-style tilt p(x)·ρ(u(x)), so the guidance term is ∇ log ρ(u(x̂₀)) — classifier guidance generalised from one class to a whole distribution.
In practice it relies on approximations: x̂₀ via Tweedie, a classifier-based ratio, a strength λ (λ = 1 is the exact Jeffrey update) and a late-time window δ; decorrelation needed λ > 1.
keyFigure: Fig. 1: overview — where classifier guidance targets a single class, Jeffrey guidance updates p(y) towards a target p*(y) via a correction term added at each diffusion step.
relevance: Jes and Pierre-Alexandre Mattei's guidance line (with Razafindralambo, Sun, Precioso): it gives a principled way to make a pretrained model match a target marginal. For you that could mean nudging a trained isoform generator so a summary statistic — e.g. the distribution of an isoform's usage fraction or of gene totals in a new cell population — matches observed data, without retraining.
brief: Focus on Sec. 2.1 (Jeffrey's rule, Eqs. 2–5) and Sec. 3.1 (the guidance term, Eqs. 12–15); the experiments can be skimmed for the λ/δ trade-off. It connects directly to the flow-matching guidance survey (fmguide) you read yesterday — place it in that taxonomy as a marginal-matching tilt. Question to keep in mind: on a discrete state space like your lattice simplex, the tilt ρ(u(x)) has no gradient — would you apply it as a rate reweighting of the CTMC generator instead (the paper's Eq. 12 hints at the non-differentiable case)?
news: No new papers from Jes or the group this week on arXiv. Worth a glance: 'Binary Discrete Diffusion' (von Rütte, Schölkopf, Hofmann et al.), a CTMC corruption kernel over candidate sets — it's in today's Discover.

extras.summary: Chapter 5 reframes a network as predicting the parameters of a distribution over outputs, and derives every loss from one recipe: choose Pr(y|θ), let the network output θ = f[x,ϕ], minimise the negative log-likelihood. Least squares, binary and softmax cross-entropy, heteroscedastic regression and multi-output losses all fall out of it, and cross-entropy is shown to equal NLL via the KL to the empirical distribution.
takeaways: The four-step recipe (Sec. 5.2): pick a distribution on the output domain, predict its parameters, minimise NLL, and at inference return the full distribution or its mode.

Least squares = Gaussian likelihood with predicted mean; binary cross-entropy = Bernoulli with a sigmoid; multiclass cross-entropy = categorical with a softmax. Predicting σ² too (with a positivity map) gives heteroscedastic regression.
Cross-entropy and NLL are the same objective (Sec. 5.7): minimising KL from the empirical distribution of Dirac deltas leaves exactly the summed log-likelihood.
pitfalls: 'Why log?' — log turns a product of per-sample likelihoods into a sum and doesn't move the argmax; it's also numerically stable.
Thinking the network outputs y rather than θ — draw the pipeline x → f → θ → Pr(y|θ); the prediction ŷ is just the mode of that distribution.
Positivity/constraints on parameters (σ², probabilities) — the network outputs unconstrained numbers, so a link function (square/softplus, sigmoid, softmax) maps them into the valid domain.
extras.links: This is the same likelihood-first view as your NB + multinomial model: gene totals get an NB likelihood and isoform splits a multinomial, i.e. exactly 'choose Pr(y|θ) for the output domain' — a nice concrete example to show students who work with counts.

extras.summary: Chapter 6 covers fitting: gradient descent, local minima and saddle points, SGD with batches and epochs, momentum (incl. Nesterov) and Adam. Adam normalises each coordinate by a running estimate of the squared gradient and adds momentum and bias correction, which makes progress even when the loss is much steeper in one direction than another.
takeaways: SGD uses a fresh random batch each step: cheaper per step, adds noise that helps escape saddle points and poor minima, and is usually run with a decaying learning-rate schedule.
Momentum averages past gradients, smoothing the trajectory and speeding progress along shallow valleys.

Adam (Eqs. 6.15–6.17) = momentum on the gradient and on its square, plus bias correction 1/(1−βᵗ); it moves roughly a fixed step per coordinate, so it is less sensitive to the initial learning rate and balances updates across layers.
pitfalls: Epoch vs iteration vs batch — one iteration = one batch gradient step; one epoch = one pass over all data (Sec. 6.2.1).
Why Adam needs bias correction — m and v start at zero, so early averages are shrunk towards zero; dividing by 1−βᵗ undoes that and its effect fades as t grows.
'Adam always wins' — it's less sensitive to learning rate but still has hyperparameters (α, β, γ, batch size); Sec. 6.5 frames these as things to search over, and students should still tune α.
extras.links: Every model in your work (flow/generator matching, VAEs) is trained this way; the noisy-gradient view also connects to the stochastic objectives in diffusion training, where each step samples data, time and noise — a good example of why SGD's noise is fine.

brief: Starting point for the whole path. Read it as a catalogue: skim the mechanisms (domain changes, localisation signals, NMD, UTR effects) and note two or three examples you'd want to look for in your own isoform data. Tomorrow's papers on proteome expansion and the Tress/Blencowe debate lean on this vocabulary.
relevance: This is the biological reason to model isoform proportions within a gene separately from gene totals, as your NB + multinomial factorisation does. The mechanisms it lists are roughly the consequences IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR annotates (domain loss, signal peptides, disordered regions, NMD sensitivity), so they are the natural way to interpret any isoform shift your generative model or scIso predicts.
summary: A long review that catalogues what alternative splicing does to the proteins it produces. It goes mechanism by mechanism: changes to binding domains and interaction partners, enzymatic activity, subcellular localisation, stability and post-translational modification. It also covers isoforms that are never translated because a premature stop codon sends them to nonsense-mediated decay.
takeaways: Splicing rarely switches a protein fully on or off. More often it adds or removes a short module (a binding motif, a localisation signal, a modification site) that changes how the protein is regulated.
Many alternative exons are short and encode disordered regions, so their effect is easy to miss if you only look at folded domains.
A large share of isoform changes act on the RNA rather than the protein, through decay or changed untranslated regions, so a shift in isoform proportions does not always mean a new protein.
